background.speaker: [target]
background.text: So first of all, thank you for having me and yes, those are daunting challenges and it's actually that issue of intertwined challenges of poverty, climate, healthcare, pandemics that I think you can't, you know, you can't disentangle these into neat little buckets and that's what led to the World Bank changing its vision from just the eradication of poverty to also adding the aspect of livable planet into it.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: The good news is it's not us trying to do this by ourselves, and I think that's a very important part of the better bank. You're not in this by yourself. Our job is to ensure we do put our resources to work, we do put our people to work, but we do it even better if we do it in partnership with other multilateral banks, with the private sector, and with governments and civil society. Because these challenges, these numbers are so large that trying to solve it by one institution or the other will not work. I think that's actually a large part of the underlying reform agenda in the bank is partnerships, both inside the bank and outside the bank. The second big part was to, you know, when you expanded the vision to include Livable Planet, the idea was to sort of open the aperture so that people could focus on what made for livability in that country. In one country, it might be a fragility conflict violence issue leading to refugees and challenges. In others, it might be a... climate issue. In a third one, it might be something to do with governance issues. And so there are different issues in each of these, and trying to find a way to do global thinking but local execution was that Livable Planet. And at that time, we added in the focus on women and young people. Women because they're half the population, and in the emerging markets, they have an even tougher time in getting the opportunity they should get. But if you did, imagine what they would do to productivity and economic growth. And so there's a plus on that. And for young people, 1.2 billion young people in the emerging markets are coming through the pipe, so to say, to be ready for a job in the next 15 years. The same countries are currently on a pathway to get about 400-odd million jobs. So there's a big gap there. And as I say all the time, focus on our destiny. So you can change it, but you have to do something to help to change that trajectory on jobs and have these young people contribute to our economic growth and future. That's all part of this Better Bank, along with the silos and the speed and the working and partnerships and all the rest of it.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: The money is an important part of that. I know that you have launched a drive or are launching a drive to replenish the International Development Association, which is the arm that serves the poorest countries. You know, some Pacific and African leaders, the prime minister of Barbados, are all pushing for that goal to be $120 billion. Is that a realistic target?

ground_truth: That's a great question. So yes, IDA is the part of our bank that goes to the 77 least sort of well-off countries in the world. And so it's truly a lifeline for them. For them, half their development money basically comes from IDA, because that's the way it works. So we're critical to their needs. And there's all kinds of good statistics around that that we could get to if we have time. But the issue of what the next replenishment should be, you've got to put it in context. 93 billion is what the current one was, IDA 20, which is the contributions from the rich countries leveraged by our bond issuing system in the private markets, thanks to our AAA rating. What we're now trying to do is to get to pass that. The African countries, President Ruto and a bunch of others, and Mayor Motley from Barbados, would like to get to the 120. Somewhere between the 93 and the 120 would be a great thing. If they get to, 120, that would be outstanding. That's what we're working on. But to get to 120, you've got to get the contributions from the rich countries to go from 24 billion to 30 billion, because that's the four is to one leverage we get on top. The challenge with that, Andrea, is that right now, a number of countries are both facing fiscal challenges. And then, of course, there's the issue of the higher dollar versus their currencies. So their contributions are under double pressure. Think of the Japanese, the yen is down 25%, from what it used to be. So just to keep pace, they got to go up 25. To go up, they got to go up 40, 50%. And that's not easy to see my way through. So we'll see. We're fighting really hard to get through this. I think we just saw Denmark issued an announcement of 40% increase. A number of other countries, the UK and Spain, have talked about going up. I think the United States is working its way through what its contribution will be. And I'm reasonably optimistic it'll be a good number. I think it's going to be a good number. I think it's going to be a good number. I think it's going to be a good number. I think it's going to be a good number. So I think we've got a few countries that are in the right direction, a few in the others. We'll see where it all shakes out.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Yes.

ground_truth: Can you tell us whether there's any news to share about reducing the lending to equity ratio? So hard off the press. Yes, that is true. We have got board approval today to change our equity to loan ratio down by another one percentage point, meaning it frees up the capacity in our balance sheet to be able to lend more. Just put it in context, there's something called the Capital Adequacy Framework in the international organization effort as part of the reform agenda when I joined. And that is meant to squeeze the balance sheet so you could take more out of it. Also meant to create new financial instruments that shareholders could contribute into. So a combination of squeezing the balance sheet through equity to loan ratios, but also through hybrid capital and portfolio guarantees has led to, I think, including what we just got today, probably close to $150 billion of more capacity to lend over the coming 7 to 10 years.

background.text: Okay, and another part of what you have been considering or what the board has been looking at are pricing changes that would affect clients. Can you say a few words about what you've done there and how that will help?

ground_truth: Yes. Again, this is IBRD principally to start with, because IDA is already either grants or deeply concessional. It's IBRD that tends to go to countries that are moving into middle income status and tends to be less concessional, but longer tenor loans. So we've done a series of things. The first thing we've done is get 50-year loans available for global public goods. You invest in climate or global health care or pandemics, you get a 50-year loan. By the very nature of a tenor of 50 years, it's deeply concessional. What we just got approved today is two or three other things in the pricing that all put together make IBRD pricing a little more attractive to these countries. We're still not as cheap as some other sources out there, but we are cheaper than at least most of the commercial sources with longer tenors. So that you put the two things together, we are an attractive source of funding. But along with that, we're also a knowledge bank. And I keep telling people there's a money bank, and a knowledge bank. And what these middle income countries really want from us is that expertise of development. We've got experiences across the world in what worked well. So we know who did good things to get coal and wood out of home cooking and convert it to solar with what things that worked in that process. We can take those learnings and take them to another country and another one and learn from each along the way. That knowledge bank, to be honest, is as valuable to these countries as the money bank. And so it's a mix of pricing and skills that we bring.
